newsitem.title: USA: Delta Air slips on profit-taking - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Delta Air slips on profit-taking - analysts.

text.p: Shares of Delta Air Lines Inc slipped after its better-than-expected third quarter earnings as investors cashed in on the recent rise in the stock price, analysts said.
Delta hit a high of 100-1/8 Thursday morning but slipped to 95-1/2 at midday, down 2-5/8 from Wednesday's close.

"Delta's had an incredibly strong run over the past couple of days. There was a lot of strength in anticipation of the earnings, based on the success of the other airlines, so when the numbers came out today, there was some profit-taking," said Timothy Ross, an analyst with SBC Warburg.
Delta's stock has risen 13.6 percent since April 1, compared with an 8.6 percent rise in the Dow Jones transportation average and a two percent increase in the Standard & Poor's 500 index.
"We have said that we wouldn't mind if people took some money off the table. Airline stocks have done so well in the past month or two," said Helane Becker, an airline analyst with Smith Barney.
"This is the peak or near the peak on earnings," she said.

Excluding charges, Delta posted third quarter earnings of $2.88 per fully diluted share, after preferred stock dividend requirements, which topped the consensus Wall Street estimate of $2.06 a share and last year's $0.80 a share.
On a net basis, Delta earned $2.47 per fully diluted share, including one-time charges, compared with a loss of $5.77 per fully diluted share last year, including charges.
Delta, the nation's third largest airline, said third quarter operating costs increased slightly due to a 22 percent rise in fuel costs.
Third quarter operating costs per available seat mile were 8.97 cents, an increase of one percent from last year.
Excluding a fuel expense increase of 22 percent, operating costs per available seat mile declined slightly from last year, it said. The airline did not elaborate.
"There was only good news. There's been some pretty virtuous cost controls. And when you strip out the fuel costs, things look really good," Ross said.
Most major U.S. carriers shattered Wall Street estimates during the March quarter as demand offset a jump in jet fuel costs, analysts said.
While demand appears to be continuing into the second quarter, analysts cautioned that airlines may not be able to continue to post record earnings.
"In order to maintain these earnings, airlines would have to see load factors increase 1.5 to 2.0 points a quarter. And that could be difficult with all the aircraft orders out there," Becker said.
